legend: Little Paul wants to learn how to play piano. He already has a melody he wants to start with. For simplicity he represented this melody as a sequence a1,a2,…,an%%ZSMJ0%% of key numbers: the more a number is, the closer it is to the right end of the piano keyboard.

Paul is very clever and knows that the essential thing is to properly assign fingers to notes he's going to play. If he chooses an inconvenient fingering, he will then waste a lot of time trying to learn how to play the melody by these fingers and he will probably not succeed.

Let's denote the fingers of hand by numbers from 1%%ZSMJ1%% to 5%%ZSMJ2%%. We call a fingering any sequence b1,…,bn%%ZSMJ3%% of fingers numbers. A fingering is convenient if for all 1≤i≤n−1%%ZSMJ4%% the following holds:
if ai<ai+1%%ZSMJ5%% then bi<bi+1%%ZSMJ6%%, because otherwise Paul needs to take his hand off the keyboard to play the (i+1)%%ZSMJ7%%-st note;
if ai>ai+1%%ZSMJ8%% then bi>bi+1%%ZSMJ9%%, because of the same;
if ai=ai+1%%ZSMJ10%% then bi≠bi+1%%ZSMJ11%%, because using the same finger twice in a row is dumb. Please note that there is ≠%%ZSMJ12%%, not =%%ZSMJ13%% between bi%%ZSMJ14%% and bi+1%%ZSMJ15%%.
Please provide any convenient fingering or find out that there is none.
input: The first line contains a single integer n%%ZSMJ16%% (1≤n≤105%%ZSMJ17%%) denoting the number of notes.
The second line contains n%%ZSMJ18%% integers a1,a2,…,an%%ZSMJ19%% (1≤ai≤2⋅105%%ZSMJ20%%) denoting the positions of notes on the keyboard.
output: If there is no convenient fingering, print −1%%ZSMJ21%%. Otherwise, print n%%ZSMJ22%% numbers b1,b2,…,bn%%ZSMJ23%%, each from 1%%ZSMJ24%% to 5%%ZSMJ25%%, denoting a convenient fingering, separated by spaces.
note: The third sample test is kinda "Non stop" song by Reflex.
